segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On the Monday, Mrs Augusta Ferris sent for her niece and Mr Dene to the parlour at the Bell, and put a paper on the table between the teacups.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: Six hundred pounds, settled on Margaret in her own name. It is a wedding gift and not a condition. I asked my question on Friday, Mr Dene, and you answered it on Friday. A thing already answered cannot be bought afterwards.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Dene looked at the paper a long moment and did not touch it.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: If I had said yes for the sake of that, you would have known it.

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: By Saturday. Take it. It is hers and not yours, which you will find a great deal more comfortable than you expect.

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: And the coal account?

segments.speaker: Mrs Augusta Ferris
segments.text: Two pounds eleven, out of the first quarter. Tell Mrs Pike you paid it yourselves, or it will be written to Bath by Thursday.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Tuesday afternoon the two of them went up to the vestry together. Mr Rowe had said he would read banns for nobody until both parties came and asked him in that room.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Miss Selby. Is it you who asks, or Mrs Pike?

segments.speaker: Miss Margaret Selby
segments.text: I ask.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Mr Dene.

segments.speaker: Mr Robert Dene
segments.text: I ask.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He wrote the two names in the book and blotted them.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: Then I am sorry to have kept you a fortnight. I had the parish's word for it and not yours.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Sunday was an ordinary Sunday, wet early and fair by the end of it. Between the second lesson and the hymn Mr Rowe published the banns of marriage between Robert Dene, schoolmaster of this parish, and Margaret Selby, spinster of this parish, and asked whether any present knew cause why they should not be joined. Nobody did. Mrs Pike looked round the church to be sure of it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: In the porch afterwards Miss Judith Vane wished Mr Rowe a good morning. He said the weather had come out better than it had promised. She agreed that it had. He hoped her brother was well, and she said her brother was perfectly well, and that was the whole of it. Each went home thinking the other extremely proud.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Pike did the whole green before dinner.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: I had it in the porch from their own mouths. I have expected it since Easter, and I said so at the time, and there is not a soul in this parish who can say I did not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She said it at the draper's and at Mrs Copp's and twice at the Bell. In no account of it was there a fortnight in which the thing had nearly come apart in her hands. She said it last at the apothecary's counter, to Miss Vane, who had the week's orders to write out and heard it to the end.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: And they will be married before Advent. You may tell your brother I said so.

segments.speaker: Miss Judith Vane
segments.text: I shall tell him exactly that.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: She wrote out the orders, and put the kettle on for her brother's dinner, and did not correct one word of it.
